blocks.raw: <Callout type="info">The 220V/60Hz electrical standard in the Philippines affects fire alarm power supply sizing and standby battery calculations. Fire alarm systems must maintain minimum 24-hour standby plus 15-minute alarm duration per NFPA 72 Chapter 10 Section 10.6, requiring robust UPS and battery backup design.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <WikiCalloutBox title="Loop Polarity in Class A SLC Circuits" variant="info">Class A SLC loops use bipolar signaling: the outgoing conductor and return conductor carry opposite polarity signals. If the outgoing wire opens, the loop detects this as a break; alarm signals continue through the return path. The control panel monitors the loop for opens and shorts and annunciates line trouble while maintaining alarm transmission capability. This is why Class A circuits cost more to install—extra copper, loop splitters, and diagnostic intelligence—but justify the cost in spaces where continuity is non-negotiable (stairwells, exits, occupancy centers).</WikiCalloutBox>

blocks.raw: <Note>Addressable detectors in the Philippines comply with NFPA 72 addressing requirements. A typical addressable loop supports 200–250 devices per SLC, depending on the panel manufacturer and protocol. Panel capacity is typically 4–8 SLCs, supporting 800–2000 addressable points per building. Water flow switches, duct detectors, and manual pull stations are each assigned unique addresses and respond to status polls independently of detector activation.</Note>

blocks.raw: <WikiCalloutBox title="NAC Load Calculations in 220V Philippine Buildings" variant="warning">Philippine fire alarm systems operate on a nominal 220V single-phase supply (some systems use 110V or 48V DC backup). NAC load calculations must account for peak demand: if the FACP supplies multiple NAC circuits and a Mass Notification System simultaneously, the total current demand can exceed the circuit capacity. A typical NAC branch in a 50-person occupancy space (say, one floor of an office building) draws 2–4 amps at alarm condition. A 16-amp FACP power supply can support 2–3 NAC circuits at full activation; beyond that, a dedicated UPS or power expansion module is required. This is a common failure point in Philippine installations where building additions increase alarm appliance load without upgrading the power supply.</WikiCalloutBox>

blocks.raw:
<Example type="scenario">A hotel in Metro Manila has a fire detection alarm triggered on the 12th floor. The FACP identifies the detector address (12-F-201, west corridor). The voice processor is programmed to:
- Announce evacuation to floors 10–14 and the ground floor (evacuation assembly point)
- Hold all elevators at the ground floor and disable them per elevator recall logic
- Play a recorded message: "Attention. Building fire alarm. Please leave the building immediately using the stairs. Do not use the elevators."
- Repeat the message every 30 seconds until the alarm is reset

Meanwhile, a parallel communication to the local fire department is sent via the central station monitoring service. The FACP logs the event (address, time, duration) for post-incident review.</Example>

blocks.raw: <Warn>A common installation error in Philippine buildings: connecting fire alarm system ground to a different point than the building's main electrical ground. This creates a ground potential difference and causes false alarms or loss of signal on SLC circuits. Fire alarm grounding must connect at the FACP's main ground, which is bonded to the building's main service entrance per electrical code (PEC).</Warn>

blocks.raw:
<Note>A building's alarm signal may reach the fire department through multiple paths:
1. The FACP sends the alarm to a central monitoring station (via SIA or Ethernet).
2. The central station verifies the alarm by calling the building's hotline to speak with an occupant or security guard.
3. The central station dispatches the BFP (Bureau of Fire Protection) or Philippine National Police (PNP) if the alarm is confirmed.
The entire process typically takes 3–5 minutes from initial alarm to fire truck dispatch, depending on central station responsiveness and building security staffing.</Note>

blocks.raw:
<Example type="scenario">A 15-story office building in Makati has a fire alarm on the 8th floor. The FACP:
1. Activates the NAC alarm (sirens and strobes on floors 7–10)
2. Routes voice evacuation to announce on floors 7–10
3. Sends elevator recall command; all 4 elevators return to lobby within 45 seconds
4. Signals BMS to shut HVAC AHUs and close smoke dampers
5. Unlocks all interior doors on all floors (access card readers disabled for egress)
6. Transmits alarm to central station: "Building ID 1234, Floor 8, Detector 8-F-201, Time 14:35"
7. Logs all events with 1-second timestamps for fire department review

The entire sequence is automatic and takes place in ~2 seconds. The FACP then holds the alarm state until a security officer or fire marshal manually resets it.</Example>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Use the 1.25 safety factor to account for battery aging (capacity degrades ~5% per year) and temperature effects (220V tropical climates like the Philippines reduce effective capacity by ~10% in hot dry seasons). A 20 Ah battery provides adequate margin for a 3–5 year service life before replacement.</Tip>
